opus-5.5.text:
I think, honestly, the biggest thing was that I genuinely loved the problems we were working on. A PhD is a long journey, and there are many moments when experiments don't work, papers get rejected, and you start to doubt yourself. What kept me going was real curiosity about the questions themselves. I wasn't just trying to finish a degree. I really wanted to know the answer.

The second thing was being willing to learn from people around me. In a strong research group you're surrounded by very smart labmates, and at first that can feel intimidating. Over time I learned to treat it as an advantage. I asked a lot of questions, joined discussions even when I didn't fully understand yet, and slowly built up my own taste for what makes a good research problem.

The third thing was learning to communicate well with my advisor. Early on I thought research meant working alone until you had something perfect to show. I later realized it's much better to share half-formed ideas early, get feedback, and adjust direction quickly. That trust and regular communication made the relationship much more productive, and it also gave me room to grow more independent over time.

And finally, resilience. Not every project succeeds, and you have to accept that. I tried to see each failure as information rather than a judgment on me. If you can keep that mindset, keep showing up, and keep improving bit by bit, then eventually things start to come together.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think a lot of it came down to luck and timing, and then a fair bit of stubbornness.

When I first joined the group, I wasn't the strongest student by any measure. There were people around me who were better at math, who read papers faster, who seemed to know exactly what they wanted to work on from day one. I didn't have that. My first year was mostly me trying to figure out what the field even was, and feeling like I was constantly behind.

What kept me there, I think, was two things. The first was that my advisor was patient in a way I didn't fully appreciate at the time. He didn't push me toward a hot topic or demand results in the first six months. He let me wander a bit, and eventually I landed on a problem that I actually cared about. Once that happened, the motivation took care of itself. I wasn't working because I was supposed to, I was working because I wanted to know the answer.

The second thing was that I learned to be okay with being slow. In research, the people who leave are often not the ones who fail, they're the ones who can't tolerate the long stretches where nothing seems to work. I had a period of almost a year where every experiment I ran was negative. I remember thinking seriously about quitting. But I had a labmate who told me something that stuck with me: the result you get after a year of failures is worth more than the one you get in a week, because nobody else was willing to sit through those failures. That reframed it for me. The frustration was the price of admission, not a sign I didn't belong.

And then, to be honest, the group culture mattered a lot. We ate lunch together, we argued about papers, people would drop by your desk when you were stuck. It's hard to leave a place where you feel like people would notice if you were gone. So if I had to summarize, I'd say: an advisor who gave me room, a problem I genuinely cared about, and a group that made the hard years feel bearable. The rest was just showing up every day.
